title: 语言模型规模规律的技术演进
content_md: # 语言模型规模规律的技术演进：机制、比较与边界 ## 摘要 本文系统梳理了语言模型规模规律的演进机制与影响。从工程试错到确立算力、数据、参数的幂律衰减规律，研究深入解释了数据流形维度与缩放系数的关系。架构上，混合专家等机制突破了密集网络算力瓶颈；数据上，多源混合配比与高频去重被证明对模型泛化稳定性至关重要。本文还讨论了微调方式与评估条件对扩展收益的改变（如U型缩放与思维链干预），最后指出了数据耗尽、分布式训练壁垒及微观能力突变所带来的极限与安全挑战。 ## 研究问题与技术前史 在深度语言模型规模规律确立之前，扩展模型的主要动机是工程实现，而非探讨计算与性能的内生规律。例如在早期字符级N-gram系统向大规模语料扩展时，研究者主要致力于利用特定的树状数据结构来压缩内存空间以支持GB级训练[2]；而在早期深度学习时代，研究者利用自然语言词频的Zipf定律降低跨GPU的通信复杂度，旨在突破硬件与显存的瓶颈以部署更大的网络[4]。这些早期方法本质上属于系统负载的工程妥协，并未触及模型容量与任务表现之间的定量关系。事实上，早在传统统计学习时期，已有研究初步推导出验证集规模比率与模型推断复杂度参数的缩放关系[1]，但现代缩放定律的缺失使得诸如循环神经网络等早期架构在面对泛化困境时，往往只能通过经验性的数据堆砌和单纯扩增模型尺寸来作为应对策略[5]。 针对这种缺乏预测性的经验扩张，研究范式随后转向了严谨量化核心计算资源的投入产出比。核心研究问题逐渐演变为：如何在不受到相互制约的前提下，精确预测计算量、数据量和参数量对模型交叉熵损失的改善程度。实证研究明确解答了这一问题，证实了在自回归语言模型中，当单一因素受限而另外两者充足时，其测试损失会随核心变量呈现跨越多个数量级的平滑幂律衰减；同时，只要维持参数总量不变，具体的网络深度和宽度对该规律的干扰极小[11]。 这一宏观经验规律确立后，进一步的研究问题深入至解释这种高度确定性的生成机制。第一种理论分支将神经网络训练视为对具有固有本征维度数据流形的回归拟合，推断出模型尺寸的增加正是通过不断细分流形来降低损失，从而产生特定的缩放指数[6]。另一种理论路径则尝试剥离复杂网络架构，利用极简玩具模型探讨学习曲线发生幂律衰减的普遍前提，旨在验证幂律究竟是数据分布的固有属性还是架构的偶然产物[26]。在此基础上，可解统计模型结合生成数据与随机特征，从理论上揭示了非线性特征映射如何承接并扩展了自然数据集的原始统计幂律谱，从而在微观机制层面重现了大型语言模型所展现的神经缩放行为[38]。这种从纯工程试错到实证量化，再到机制建模的演进，构成了后续探讨不同架构和数据配比缩放差异的技术前史。 ## 架构、表示与训练目标 语言模型规模规律的底层机制可映射至数据流形的内在维度。理论表明，网络测试损失的缩放指数受流形内在维度控制（即$\alpha \approx 4/d$）[55]。不同架构的归纳偏置会显著改变这种缩放行为。实证研究显示，尽管各类架构在特定计算区间互有胜负，但标准Transformer跨规模的缩放系数表现最为稳健[56]。同时，其他序列架构提供了正交的缩放优势：例如，勒让德记忆单元（LMU）在中小型规模下展现出极高的数据效率，仅需Transformer十分之一的token即可达到同等准确率[23]；而通过检索表扩展n-gram嵌入（LookupLM），可在保持前向传播浮点运算量不变、零额外推理计算的前提下，大幅增加模型容量与长尾表现[27]。 为突破密集架构的计算平方瓶颈，混合专家（MoE）架构通过条件计算解耦了参数量与算力消耗。GShard率先在机器翻译中验证了该机制，实现了千亿级参数的高效自动分片扩展[10]。在自回归语言模型中，MoE相比密集架构展现出非线性的效率替代：在中等训练预算下，MoE仅需约四分之一的算力即可匹配密集模型性能，尽管该效率差距会随规模上升而收窄[16]。为解决极端扩展下的通信与数值不稳定，Switch Transformer精简了路由算法并引入低精度（bfloat16）训练格式[34]；这为GLaM等架构奠定了基础，使其在达到1.2万亿参数时，仅消耗GPT-3三分之一的训练能耗便实现了更优的小样本性能[18]。此外，针对随机初始化专家网络导致的早期路由震荡，EvoMoE创新了从密集到稀疏的门控演化机制，在单一专家成熟后再分化并稀疏激活，从根本上改善了收敛稳定性[17]。 表示能力随规模的扩展深度依赖于训练目标的演进。在迁移学习机制中，预训练语言模型所传递的知识在数学上表现为对下游微调数据量的等效倍增，其缩放指数直接反映了架构在目标分布上的泛化度[33]。对监督机器翻译等任务，交叉熵损失随非嵌入参数量与数据的幂律下降，能确定性地转化为BLEU分数的指数级提升[14]。当大幅扩展多语言掩码语言建模（MLM）目标时（如107亿参数的XLM-R XXL），不仅不损害高资源语言性能，还能显著增强极低资源下的跨语言零样本表示能力[24]。指令微调（Flan）进一步扩展了表示的可用性，系统性扩充任务数量并融入思维链（CoT）数据，能大幅提升多种大模型的少样本泛化与推理表现[52]。此外，扩展表示亦可绕过参数更新：通过训练辅助目标动态检索当前上下文窗口外的“远古历史”片段并直接拼接，可在完全不更新核心语言模型参数的条件下显著降低困惑度[19]。 ## 数据规模、配比与训练稳定性 语言模型规模规律的研究不仅局限于参数扩张，数据规模的有效性、混合配比的策略以及由此引发的训练稳定性问题同样构成了核心演进主线。随着预训练语料从单一来源向多源异构扩展，如何预测和优化数据组合成为重要议题。 在数据配比与泛化性能的机制方面，[28]通过最优实验设计理论推导出泛化误差的有理函数近似，将多数据源混合下的模型性能预测转化为学习问题，从而在大幅外推条件下也能有效预估性能。针对特定领域的配比，[36]基于法律判决数据集CaseHOLD的研究表明，当目标任务与预训练语料展现出充分的相似性与领域特异性时，投入大量资源进行特定领域预训练相比通用语料预训练（如基于谷歌图书和维基百科的通用BERT）能带来显著的性能增益。此外，为了让语言模型更好地捕获历史或地理分布的异质性，[48]并未采用直接切分数据集分别训练的传统方法，而是通过将元数据作为特殊Token直接注入掩码语言模型（MLM）的输入序列中。该机制表明，在特定比例（如25%）下对元数据进行掩码训练，不仅能引导模型学习文本内容与元数据的深层关联，还避免了为不同数据子集进行多次独立训练的成本。 数据重复度是影响大语言模型训练稳定性的另一个微观关键因素。[54]通过将宏观缩放规律与微观可解释性机制相结合指出，当预训练语料中存在少量被高频重复的数据时（例如0.1%的数据重复100次），会诱发强烈的基于轮次的“双重下降”（double descent）现象，导致训练中途测试损失异常上升。这种性能严重退化源于模型将大量表征容量耗费在记忆重复数据上，从而对负责泛化能力的内部机制（如归纳头）造成不成比例的破坏。 在数据组织结构的配比上，为了赋予自回归语言模型中间填充（FIM）能力，[40]通过文档级或上下文级的随机变换，将输入文本拆分为前缀、后缀和中间部分。实验证实，即使在预训练数据中混入高达50%的FIM变换格式数据，也完全不会对模型原有的从左到右自回归生成损失产生破坏。这证明了合理规划数据格式的混合比例，可以在不损失基础泛化性能的前提下，以零额外代价解锁模型的结构化生成新能力。 ## 扩展规律和资源约束 语言模型规模规律的研究已从纯预训练阶段延伸至全生命周期及复杂资源约束下的机制演进。早期扩展规律曾假设自回归语言模型的性能主要依赖参数总规模而弱依赖网络形状。然而针对预训练-微调范式，实证表明下游微调任务的性能对模型形状高度敏感，且小模型的扩展经验无法直接迁移至大计算资源区间[30]。在给定计算预算下，将算力用于扩大模型尺寸的边际收益显著高于单纯延长训练步数，相较而言增加批次大小比增加步数更有益[12]。更进一步，针对特定架构的自回归Transformer，其解码器参数量与模型困惑度呈现出极高的秩相关性，这一规律直接促成了免训练的零成本架构搜索代理，大幅消减了模型结构搜索的算力消耗[46]。 随着模型向千亿参数演进，算力与显存瓶颈的物理表现发生转变。研究指出，在混合精度与检查点等机制支持下，限制大模型扩展的实质壁垒并非普遍假定的“内存墙”，而是极长的训练周期[25]。为突破时间与空间双重约束，分布式训练分化出多维并行与异构卸载两大优化分支。针对极大规模扩展，Megatron-Turing NLG 530B等模型采用深度融合数据、张量与流水线的3D并行架构跨节点扩展[58]；结合分层梯度累积与模块化流水线并行，可大幅降低分布式数据移动，使常规互联网络亦能承载原需高带宽通信的训练数据流[25]。针对单节点显存受限场景，ZeRO-Offload将优化器状态和参数更新计算卸载至CPU内存，并设计单步延迟参数更新机制（DPU）使得CPU与GPU计算重叠，从而在隐蔽通信开销的同时突破单卡显存极限[37]。 在面临极端序列长度或特殊分布式约束时，架构本身的运行机制需定向改造。处理超长上下文时，交错局部块与全局词元结合的稀疏注意力机制，配合先短序列后长序列的两阶段预训练适应，能在控制额外显存的同时有效提升长序列建模能力[45]。计算图动态性强的递归神经网络文法（RNNG）则通过跨句张量重组机制化解了传统批处理困难，实现了匹配计算硬件的张量并行扩展[15]。此外，在跨设备去中心化计算（如联邦学习）中，模型的拓扑压缩机制会直接影响扩展稳定性；例如采用知识蒸馏压缩的学生模型在多客户端联邦平均更新时，较其未蒸馏的庞大基础模型更容易出现收敛迟缓甚至性能崩溃[31]，凸显了分布式扩展下模型内部信息流转的脆弱性。 ## 实验证据与方法比较 语言模型规模规律的评估标准在演进过程中，逐渐暴露出传统单一指标的局限性。早期的主流指标如困惑度（Perplexity）高度依赖于词频统计，容易受到自然语言中齐夫定律（Zipfian distribution）高频词的干扰，从而掩盖了模型在低频词或深层语义上的真实表现[7]。为了更细粒度地评估模型的生成质量，研究表明需要考察模型生成文本与真实自然语言在统计分布（如长度、停用词等）上的拟合度，并且这种拟合度受采样策略和架构的显著影响[22]。为此，评估基准逐渐从扁平化的数据集堆叠，演进为包含“语言能力-任务-数据集”层级架构[13]以及按难度分级的多任务生成评估体系[9]。 在不同对照条件下，模型规模扩展呈现出复杂的、甚至冲突的性能曲线。架构差异与下游任务适配方法是决定缩放规律形态的关键变量。在机器翻译等任务中，不同掩码机制的语言模型与编码器-解码器架构在小参数规模下表现出显著的性能鸿沟，但随着参数量级向大基数扩展，这种由架构引入的性能差距会逐渐缩小[43]。另一方面，针对分布外数据的组合泛化任务，模型扩展并非总是带来收益：全参数微调通常表现出平坦甚至负向的缩放曲线（大模型更易出现特定类型的过拟合），而提示微调（Prompt tuning）和上下文学习（In-context learning）则能维持正向的规模扩展收益[42]。 最为典型的冲突结果体现在“逆向缩放”（Inverse Scaling）现象及其机制中。部分基准测试曾指出某些任务性能随参数增加而下降。然而，当规模进一步扩大时，这种下降往往演变为“U型缩放”曲线[44]。该机制的本质在于任务包含了“真实任务”和“干扰任务”：中等规模模型具备了执行干扰任务的能力导致总体性能受损，只有大型模型才具备忽略干扰解决真实任务的涌现能力[44]。此外，这种曲线对评估对照条件极度敏感。在复杂推理任务中，若引入思维链（Chain-of-Thought）提示，原本在仅输出答案（Answer-only）条件下呈现平坦或逆向缩放的曲线会转为正向扩展，这证明了次优的提示对照会严重低估模型的真实能力[39][44]。 ## 局限、效率与开放问题 规模规律的预测可靠性高度依赖拟合策略，相较于简单的插值，基于外推损失的方法能更准确地预测未见规模的性能[51]。尽管泛化误差随数据量呈现幂律递减，但模型最优参数量级与数据量之间实为亚线性扩展关系[3]。更为严峻的是数据供给极限，高质量文本数据可能在短期内耗尽，打破依赖海量数据扩展的现有范式[60]。此外，单纯的数据扩展会放大分布缺陷：当语料未经过滤时，规模扩大会导致生成更多攻击性文本[29]；在真实性问答中，由于模型过度拟合训练集中的“模仿性谬误”，更大规模的模型反而表现出更低的真实性[35]。同时，评估泄露问题也随着数据规模扩张而加剧，必须通过量化验证评估块与训练数据的重叠比例，以剥离纯记忆对规模收益的虚假贡献[20]。 在环境与算力成本日益高昂的压力下[21]，模型扩展暴露出诸多工程效率瓶颈。受限于硬件显存瓶颈与多维并行策略的节点跨越成本，参数规模在特定区间（如20B至70B）出现了由于成本效益骤降而导致的“参数真空”现象[47]。为在资源约束下突破基准缩放曲线，研究者在训练与部署端探索了多套机制：在训练阶段，利用混合降噪目标（Mixture-of-Denoisers）进行极少步数的持续训练，能够在不增加参数量的前提下显著提升下游性能曲线[57]；在推理阶段，动态条件计算架构允许模型根据不同计算预算实时切断或激活特定执行路径[8]，而针对混合专家（MoE）模型，将专家权重进行4位整数对称量化并结合推理时的融合反量化计算，有效化解了显存带宽限制并维持了计算精度[59]。然而，并非所有底层优化都能成功跨越规模鸿沟，旨在打破反向传播串行约束的直接反馈对齐（DFA）机制在因果解码器中始终无法获得超越反向传播的计算效率[53]，且常用于视觉的动态稀疏训练方法（如RigL）在大型语言模型中亦未能兑现降低浮点运算的理论预期[32]。 规模规律最深层的理论失效在于其无法解释预训练损失与下游特定任务间的“不可预测性”。尽管整体语言建模的交叉熵损失随计算规模平滑下降，但模型在复杂算术、多步推理等任务上的准确率却会在跨越某计算阈值时呈现不连续的突变式跃升[49]。这种宏观指标平滑与微观能力突变的并存机制[50]，部分源于精确匹配等离散指标未能反映出目标序列对数似然在小规模时的持续改善[41]。由于这种突发能力无法通过小规模模型的基准表现进行外推，其不仅为大模型的安全部署与风险审查带来了盲区[50]，也使得揭示模型如何将量变转化为涌现能力的微观机制，成为当前规律研究中最具挑战性的开放问题。 ## 结论 模型规模规律确立了资源投入与性能改善的强相关性，但单纯的规模扩张正面临多重瓶颈。架构创新与异构分布式卸载技术虽部分缓解了算力与内存限制，但高质量语料的临近枯竭、微观涌现能力的不可预测性，以及次优评估导致的性能低估，均凸显出现有范式的局限。未来大模型演进需超越单纯的数据与参数堆砌，深入探索特定数据的转化效率、动态条件计算及可解释机制，以实现在资源受限条件下的安全可控发展。 ## 参考文献 [1] Isabelle M Guyon. source_intervals.text: A Scaling Law for the Validation-Set Training-Set Size Ratio We address the problem of determining what fraction of the training set should be reserved as development test set or validation set. We determine that the ratio of the validation set size over the training set size scales like the square root of two complexity parameters: the complexity of the second level of inference (minimizing the validation error) over the complexity of the rst level of inference (minimizing the error rate on the training set).

source_intervals.text: Scaling High-Order Character Language Models to Gigabytes We describe the implementation steps required to scale high-order character language models to gigabytes of training data without pruning. Our online models build character-level PAT trie structures on the fly using heavily data-unfolded implementations of an mutable daughter maps with a long integer count interface. Terminal nodes are shared. Character 8-gram training runs at 200,000 characters per second and allows online tuning of hyperparameters. Our compiled models precompute all probability estimates for observed n-grams and all interpolation parameters, along with suffix pointers to speedup context computations from proportional to n-gram length to a constant. source_intervals.text: Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically Deep learning (DL) creates impactful advances following a virtuous recipe: model architecture search, creating large training data sets, and scaling computation. It is widely believed that growing training sets and models should improve accuracy and result in better products. As DL application domains grow, we would like a deeper understanding of the relationships between training set size, computational scale, and model accuracy improvements to advance the state-of-the-art. This paper presents a large scale empirical characterization of generalization error and model size growth as training sets grow. We introduce a methodology for this measurement and test four machine learning domains: machine translation, language modeling, image processing, and speech recognition. Our empirical results show power-law generalization error scaling across a breadth of factors, resulting in power-law exponents---the"steepness"of the learning curve---yet to be explained by theoretical work. Further, model improvements only shift the error but do not appear to affect the power-law exponent. We also show that model size scales sublinearly with data size. These scaling relationships have significant implications on deep learning research, practice, and systems. They can assist model debugging, setting accuracy targets, and decisions about data set

growth. They can also guide computing system design and underscore the importance of continued computational scaling. source_intervals.text: Language Modeling at Scale We show how Zipf's Law can be used to scale up language modeling (LM) to take advantage of more training data and more GPUs. LM plays a key role in many important natural language applications such as speech recognition and machine translation. Scaling up LM is important since it is widely accepted by the community that there is no data like more data. Eventually, we would like to train on terabytes (TBs) of text (trillions of words). Modern training methods are far from this goal, because of various bottlenecks, especially memory (within GPUs) and communication (across GPUs). This paper shows how Zipf's Law can address these bottlenecks by grouping parameters for common words and character sequences, because $U \ll N$, where $U$ is the number of unique words (types) and $N$ is the size of the training set (tokens). For a local batch size $K$ with $G$ GPUs and a $D$-dimension embedding matrix, we reduce the original per-GPU memory and communication asymptotic complexity from $\Theta(GKD)$ to $\Theta(GK + UD)$. Empirically, we find $U \propto (GK)^{0.64}$ on four publicly available large datasets. When we scale up the number of GPUs to 64, a factor of 8, training time speeds up by factors up to 6.7$\times$ (for character LMs) and 6.3$\times$ (for word LMs) with negligible loss of accuracy. Abstract
When data is plentiful, the loss achieved by well-trained neural networks scales as a powerlaw L ∝ N −α in the number of network parameters N . This empirical scaling law holds
for a wide variety of data modalities, and may persist over many orders of magnitude. The
scaling law can be explained if neural models are effectively just performing regression
on a data manifold of intrinsic dimension d. This simple theory predicts that the scaling exponents α ≈ 4/d for cross-entropy and mean-squared error losses. We confirm the
theory by independently measuring the intrinsic dimension and the scaling exponents in a
teacher/student framework, where we can study a variety of d and α by dialing the properties of random teacher networks. We also test the theory with CNN image classifiers on
several datasets and with GPT-type language models.

source_intervals.text: Are Some Words Worth More than Others? Current evaluation metrics for language modeling and generation rely heavily on the accuracy of predicted (or generated) words as compared to a reference ground truth. While important, token-level accuracy only captures one aspect of a language model’s behavior, and ignores linguistic properties of words that may allow some mis-predicted tokens to be useful in practice. Furthermore, statistics directly tied to prediction accuracy (including perplexity) may be confounded by the Zipfian nature of written language, as the majority of the prediction attempts will occur with frequently-occurring types. A model’s performance may vary greatly between high- and low-frequency words, which in practice could lead to failure modes such as repetitive and dull generated text being produced by a downstream consumer of a language model. To address this, we propose two new intrinsic evaluation measures within the framework of a simple word prediction task that are designed to give a more holistic picture of a language model’s performance. We evaluate several commonly-used large English language models using our proposed metrics, and demonstrate that our approach reveals functional differences in performance between the models that are obscured by more traditional metrics. source_intervals.text: GShard: Scaling Giant Models with Conditional Computation and Automatic Sharding Neural network scaling has been critical for improving the model quality in many real-world machine learning applications with vast amounts of training data and compute. Although this trend of scaling is affirmed to be a sure-fire approach for better model quality, there are challenges on the path such as the computation cost, ease of programming, and efficient implementation on parallel devices. GShard is a module composed of a set of lightweight annotation APIs and an extension to the XLA compiler. It provides an elegant way to express a wide range of parallel computation patterns with minimal changes to the existing model code. GShard enabled us to scale up multilingual neural machine translation Transformer model with Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts beyond 600 billion parameters using automatic sharding. We demonstrate that such a giant model can efficiently be trained on 2048 TPU v3 accelerators in 4 days to achieve far superior quality for translation from 100 languages to English compared to the prior art. source_intervals.text: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models We study empirical scaling laws for language model performance on the cross-entropy loss. The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. This paper presents a detailed empirical study of how autoregressive MoE language models scale in comparison with dense models in a wide range of settings: in- and out-of-domain language modeling, zero- and few-shot priming, and full-shot fine-tuning. At more modest training budgets, MoEs can match the performance of dense models using $\sim$4 times less compute. Overall, this performance gap varies greatly across tasks and domains, suggesting that MoE and dense models generalize differently in ways that are worthy of future study. source_intervals.text: Language Model Evaluation Beyond Perplexity We propose an alternate approach to quantifying how well language models learn natural language: we ask how well they match the statistical tendencies of natural language. To answer this question, we analyze whether text generated from language models exhibits the statistical tendencies present in the human-generated text on which they were trained. We provide a framework–paired with significance tests–for evaluating the fit of language models to these trends. We find that neural language models appear to learn only a subset of the tendencies considered, but align much more closely with empirical trends than proposed theoretical distributions (when present). Further, the fit to different distributions is highly-dependent on both model architecture and generation strategy. As concrete examples, text generated under the nucleus sampling scheme adheres more closely to the type–token relationship of natural language than text produced using standard ancestral sampling; text from LSTMs reflects the natural language distributions over length, stopwords, and symbols surprisingly well. source_intervals.text: Layered gradient accumulation and modular pipeline parallelism: fast and efficient training of large language models The advent of the transformer has sparked a quick growth in the size of language models, far outpacing hardware improvements. (Dense) transformers are expected to reach the trillion-parameter scale in the near future, for which training requires thousands or even tens of thousands of GPUs. We investigate the challenges of training at this scale and beyond on commercially available hardware. In particular, we analyse the shortest possible training time for different configurations of distributed training, leveraging empirical scaling laws for language models to estimate the optimal (critical) batch size. Contrary to popular belief, we find no evidence for a memory wall, and instead argue that the real limitation -- other than the cost -- lies in the training duration. In addition to this analysis, we introduce two new methods, \textit{layered gradient accumulation} and \textit{modular pipeline parallelism}, which together cut the shortest training time by half. The methods also reduce data movement, lowering the network requirement to a point where a fast InfiniBand connection is not necessary. This increased network efficiency also improve on the methods introduced with the ZeRO optimizer, reducing the memory usage to a tiny fraction of the available GPU memory.

source_intervals.text: Lookup-Table Recurrent Language Models for Long Tail Speech Recognition We introduce Lookup-Table Language Models (LookupLM), a method for scaling up the size of RNN language models with only a constant increase in the floating point operations, by increasing the expressivity of the embedding table. In particular, we instantiate an (additional) embedding table which embeds the previous n-gram token sequence, rather than a single token. This allows the embedding table to be scaled up arbitrarily -- with a commensurate increase in performance -- without changing the token vocabulary. Since embeddings are sparsely retrieved from the table via a lookup; increasing the size of the table adds neither extra operations to each forward pass nor extra parameters that need to be stored on limited GPU/TPU memory. We explore scaling n-gram embedding tables up to nearly a billion parameters. When trained on a 3-billion sentence corpus, we find that LookupLM improves long tail log perplexity by 2.44 and long tail WER by 23.4% on a downstream speech recognition task over a standard RNN language model baseline, an improvement comparable to a scaling up the baseline by 6.2x the number of floating point operations. Introduction Improving the decoding of rare words or sequences is an ongoing problem in natural language tasks. For example, speech recognition systems misrecognize many legitimate tok

ary necessitates increasing the token vocabulary and, undesirably, the softmax parameters. Further, often a specific token vocabulary (e.g. a particular 4096-wordpiece vocabulary) is required in order to be compatible with downstream tasks (e.g. for shallow fusion with a speech model which has that vocabulary). Yet, scaling up the

embedding vocabulary has a key advantage: embedding lookups are sparse and lightweight. For instance in language models, only a single fixed-dimensional vector from the embedding table corresponding to the current token must be retrieved from memory at each step. In contrast to "sparse" parameters such as embeddings, other parameters are "dense": they are involved at each step (an exception is conditional computation models, see §1.1), and consequently must be stored on limited, high-bandwidth GPU/TPU memory. Sparse parameters can potentially be stored on off-chip memory, such as on CPU memory, disk, or even a remote parameter server [14], and retrieved in a lightweight fashion (typically a few kilobytes per embedding vector). Since the vocabulary size of the embedding table has no effect on the number of lookups or operations involved in each forward pass, it means that the embedding vocabulary can be scaled up arbitrarily with no increase in compute. source_intervals.text: Model Performance Scaling with Multiple Data Sources Real-world machine learning systems are often trained using a mix of data sources with varying cost and quality. Understanding how the size and composition of a training dataset affect model performance is critical for advancing our understanding of generalization, as well as designing more effective data collection policies. We show that there is a simple scaling law that predicts the loss incurred by a model even under varying dataset composition. Our work expands recent observations of scaling laws for log-linear generalization error in the i.i.d setting and uses this to cast model performance prediction as a learning problem. Using the theory of optimal experimental design, we derive a simple rational function approximation to generalization error that can be fitted using a few model training runs. Our approach can achieve highly accurate (r ≈ .9) predictions of model performance under substantial extrapolation in two different standard supervised learning tasks and is accurate (r ≈ .83) on more challenging machine translation and question answering tasks where many baselines achieve worse-thanrandom performance.

We find the pre-training dataset significantly conditions the quality of the outputs, with common datasets such as OSCAR leading to low-quality offensive text. We evaluate our models on discriminative and generative tasks in French, comparing to other state-of-the-art French and multilingual models, and reaching the state of the art in the abstract summarization task. source_intervals.text: Scale Efficiently: Insights from Pre-training and Fine-tuning Transformers There remain many open questions pertaining to the scaling behaviour of Transformer architectures. These scaling decisions and findings can be critical, as training runs often come with an associated computational cost which have both financial and/or environmental impact. The goal of this paper is to present scaling insights from pretraining and finetuning Transformers. While Kaplan et al. presents a comprehensive study of the scaling behaviour of Transformer language models, the scope is only on the upstream (pretraining) loss. Therefore, it is still unclear if these set of findings transfer to downstream task within the context of the pretrain-finetune paradigm. The key findings of this paper are as follows: (1) we show that aside from only the model size, model shape matters for downstream fine-tuning, (2) scaling protocols operate differently at different compute regions, (3) widely adopted T5-base and T5-large sizes are Pareto-inefficient. To this end, we present improved scaling protocols whereby our redesigned models achieve similar downstream fine-tuning quality while having 50\% fewer parameters and training 40\% faster compared to the widely adopted T5-base model. We publicly release over 100 pretrained checkpoints of different T5 configurations to facilitate future research and analysis. INTR

ear in mind that this is a model which is effectively smaller in parameters and has 10% less FLOPs. CONCLUSION In this paper, we present several important findings pertaining to training and practical usage of efficient transformer architectures. Specifically, we discovered that scaling laws differ in upstream and downstream. Contrary to prior work (Kaplan et al., 2020), we emphasize the importance of model shape for ensuring strong downstream performance. Next, we also discovered that scaling happens rather differently at different compute regions and scaling a small model would behave differently from scaling a large model. We highlight that this has implications since model development in a certain compute region could potentially not transfer to another compute region. We go on to show that not all model knobs are created equal, i.e., some knobs (such as depth) has a larger impact on the Pareto-frontier. Finally, we propose a simple but highly effective improved scaling protocol. With this strategy, we obtain models with similar downstream finetuning quality while having 50% fewer parameters and/or training 40% faster.

source_intervals.text: Scaling Laws for Transfer We study empirical scaling laws for transfer learning between distributions in an unsupervised, fine-tuning setting. When we train increasingly large neural networks from-scratch on a fixed-size dataset, they eventually become data-limited and stop improving in performance (cross-entropy loss). When we do the same for models pre-trained on a large language dataset, the slope in performance gains is merely reduced rather than going to zero. We calculate the effective data"transferred"from pre-training by determining how much data a transformer of the same size would have required to achieve the same loss when training from scratch. In other words, we focus on units of data while holding everything else fixed. source_intervals.text: TruthfulQA: Measuring How Models Mimic Human Falsehoods We propose a benchmark to measure whether a language model is truthful in generating answers to questions. The benchmark comprises 817 questions that span 38 categories, including health, law, finance and politics. We crafted questions that some humans would answer falsely due to a false belief or misconception. To perform well, models must avoid generating false answers learned from imitating human texts. We tested GPT-3, GPT-Neo/J, GPT-2 and a T5-based model. The best model was truthful on 58% of questions, while human performance was 94%. Models generated many false answers that mimic popular misconceptions and have the potential to deceive humans. The largest models were generally the least truthful. This contrasts with other NLP tasks, where performance improves with model size. However, this result is expected if false answers are learned from the training distribution. We suggest that scaling up models alone is less promising for improving truthfulness than fine-tuning using training objectives other than imitation of text from the web. ZeRO-Offload enables large model training by offloading data and compute to CPU. source_intervals.text: A Solvable Model of Neural Scaling Laws Large language models with a huge number of parameters, when trained on near internet-sized number of tokens, have been empirically shown to obey neural scaling laws: specifically, their performance behaves predictably as a power law in either parameters or dataset size until bottlenecked by the other resource. source_intervals.text: Machine Learning Model Sizes and the Parameter Gap We study trends in model size of notable machine learning systems over time using a curated dataset. From 1950 to 2018, model size in language models increased steadily by seven orders of magnitude. The trend then accelerated, with model size increasing by another five orders of magnitude in just 4 years from 2018 to 2022. Vision models grew at a more constant pace, totaling 7 orders of magnitude of growth between 1950 and 2022. We also identify that, since 2020, there have been many language models below 20B parameters, many models above 70B parameters, but a scarcity of models in the 20-70B parameter range. We refer to that scarcity as the parameter gap. We provide some stylized facts about the parameter gap and propose a few hypotheses to explain it. The explanations we favor are: (a) increasing model size beyond 20B parameters requires adopting different parallelism techniques, which makes mid-sized models less cost-effective, (b) GPT-3 was one order of magnitude larger than previous language models, and researchers afterwards primarily experimented with bigger models to outperform it. While these dynamics likely exist, and we believe they play some role in generating the gap, we don't have high confidence that there are no other, more important dynamics at play. I. In addition, we can generate some predictions from our hypotheses on the parameter gap: • Hardware limitations might cause discontinuities or bottlenecks in scaling by limiting model size rather than compute. For example, 3,072 GPUs can be used to train a trillion parameter Transformer [12]. Summit, the 4th top supercomputer as of July 2022, has 27,648 GPUs. So training dense language models beyond 10T parameters will likely require using non-GPU memory, bigger supercomputers (which take time to build), or communication between supercomputers. • After a sudden jump in the largest model size used for a given task or benchmark, we should expect to stop seeing smaller notable models competing in the same tasks or benchmarks, at least in domains with robust scaling laws. This implies that a single well-funded actor can suddenly change the dynamics of AI research. In particular, by (a) causing less resourceful actors to stop working on a given task or benchmark since the well-funded actor jumped to too large a model size to be worth trying to compete with, (b) causing other well funded actors to increase their spending if they want to remain competitive. source_intervals.text: Scaling Laws Beyond Backpropagation Alternatives to backpropagation have long been studied to better understand how biological brains may learn. Recently, they have also garnered interest as a way to train neural networks more efficiently. By relaxing constraints inherent to backpropagation (e.g., symmetric feedforward and feedback weights, sequential updates), these methods enable promising prospects, such as local learning. However, the tradeoffs between different methods in terms of final task performance, convergence speed, and ultimately compute and data requirements are rarely outlined. In this work, we use scaling laws to study the ability of Direct Feedback Alignment~(DFA) to train causal decoder-only Transformers efficiently. Scaling laws provide an overview of the tradeoffs implied by a modeling decision, up to extrapolating how it might transfer to increasingly large models. We find that DFA fails to offer more efficient scaling than backpropagation: there is never a regime for which the degradation in loss incurred by using DFA is worth the potential reduction in compute budget. Our finding comes at variance with previous beliefs in the alternative training methods community, and highlights the need for holistic empirical approaches to better understand modeling decisions. source_intervals.text: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. source_intervals.text: Scaling Laws from the Data Manifold Dimension When data is plentiful, the test loss achieved by well-trained neural networks scales as a power-law L ∝ N−α in the number of network parameters N . This empirical scaling law holds for a wide variety of data modalities, and may persist over many orders of magnitude. The scaling law can be explained if neural models are effectively just performing regression on a data manifold of intrinsic dimension d. This simple theory predicts that the scaling exponents α ≈ 4/d for cross-entropy and mean-squared error losses. We confirm the theory by independently measuring the intrinsic dimension and the scaling exponents in a teacher/student framework, where we can study a variety of d and α by dialing the properties of random teacher networks. We also test the theory with CNN image classifiers on several datasets and with GPT-type language models.

An analysis of the limits of scaling datasets in Machine Learning We analyze the growth of dataset sizes used in machine learning for natural language processing and computer vision, and extrapolate these using two methods; using the historical growth rate and estimating the compute-optimal dataset size for future predicted compute budgets. sections.title: 研究问题与技术前史
sections.body:
在深度语言模型规模规律确立之前，扩展模型的主要动机是工程实现，而非探讨计算与性能的内生规律。例如在早期字符级N-gram系统向大规模语料扩展时，研究者主要致力于利用特定的树状数据结构来压缩内存空间以支持GB级训练[2]；而在早期深度学习时代，研究者利用自然语言词频的Zipf定律降低跨GPU的通信复杂度，旨在突破硬件与显存的瓶颈以部署更大的网络[4]。这些早期方法本质上属于系统负载的工程妥协，并未触及模型容量与任务表现之间的定量关系。事实上，早在传统统计学习时期，已有研究初步推导出验证集规模比率与模型推断复杂度参数的缩放关系[1]，但现代缩放定律的缺失使得诸如循环神经网络等早期架构在面对泛化困境时，往往只能通过经验性的数据堆砌和单纯扩增模型尺寸来作为应对策略[5]。

针对这种缺乏预测性的经验扩张，研究范式随后转向了严谨量化核心计算资源的投入产出比。核心研究问题逐渐演变为：如何在不受到相互制约的前提下，精确预测计算量、数据量和参数量对模型交叉熵损失的改善程度。实证研究明确解答了这一问题，证实了在自回归语言模型中，当单一因素受限而另外两者充足时，其测试损失会随核心变量呈现跨越多个数量级的平滑幂律衰减；同时，只要维持参数总量不变，具体的网络深度和宽度对该规律的干扰极小[11]。

这一宏观经验规律确立后，进一步的研究问题深入至解释这种高度确定性的生成机制。第一种理论分支将神经网络训练视为对具有固有本征维度数据流形的回归拟合，推断出模型尺寸的增加正是通过不断细分流形来降低损失，从而产生特定的缩放指数[6]。另一种理论路径则尝试剥离复杂网络架构，利用极简玩具模型探讨学习曲线发生幂律衰减的普遍前提，旨在验证幂律究竟是数据分布的固有属性还是架构的偶然产物[26]。在此基础上，可解统计模型结合生成数据与随机特征，从理论上揭示了非线性特征映射如何承接并扩展了自然数据集的原始统计幂律谱，从而在微观机制层面重现了大型语言模型所展现的神经缩放行为[38]。这种从纯工程试错到实证量化，再到机制建模的演进，构成了后续探讨不同架构和数据配比缩放差异的技术前史。

sections.title: 架构、表示与训练目标
sections.body:
语言模型规模规律的底层机制可映射至数据流形的内在维度。理论表明，网络测试损失的缩放指数受流形内在维度控制（即$\alpha \approx 4/d$）[55]。不同架构的归纳偏置会显著改变这种缩放行为。实证研究显示，尽管各类架构在特定计算区间互有胜负，但标准Transformer跨规模的缩放系数表现最为稳健[56]。同时，其他序列架构提供了正交的缩放优势：例如，勒让德记忆单元（LMU）在中小型规模下展现出极高的数据效率，仅需Transformer十分之一的token即可达到同等准确率[23]；而通过检索表扩展n-gram嵌入（LookupLM），可在保持前向传播浮点运算量不变、零额外推理计算的前提下，大幅增加模型容量与长尾表现[27]。

为突破密集架构的计算平方瓶颈，混合专家（MoE）架构通过条件计算解耦了参数量与算力消耗。GShard率先在机器翻译中验证了该机制，实现了千亿级参数的高效自动分片扩展[10]。在自回归语言模型中，MoE相比密集架构展现出非线性的效率替代：在中等训练预算下，MoE仅需约四分之一的算力即可匹配密集模型性能，尽管该效率差距会随规模上升而收窄[16]。为解决极端扩展下的通信与数值不稳定，Switch Transformer精简了路由算法并引入低精度（bfloat16）训练格式[34]；这为GLaM等架构奠定了基础，使其在达到1.2万亿参数时，仅消耗GPT-3三分之一的训练能耗便实现了更优的小样本性能[18]。此外，针对随机初始化专家网络导致的早期路由震荡，EvoMoE创新了从密集到稀疏的门控演化机制，在单一专家成熟后再分化并稀疏激活，从根本上改善了收敛稳定性[17]。

表示能力随规模的扩展深度依赖于训练目标的演进。在迁移学习机制中，预训练语言模型所传递的知识在数学上表现为对下游微调数据量的等效倍增，其缩放指数直接反映了架构在目标分布上的泛化度[33]。对监督机器翻译等任务，交叉熵损失随非嵌入参数量与数据的幂律下降，能确定性地转化为BLEU分数的指数级提升[14]。当大幅扩展多语言掩码语言建模（MLM）目标时（如107亿参数的XLM-R XXL），不仅不损害高资源语言性能，还能显著增强极低资源下的跨语言零样本表示能力[24]。指令微调（Flan）进一步扩展了表示的可用性，系统性扩充任务数量并融入思维链（CoT）数据，能大幅提升多种大模型的少样本泛化与推理表现[52]。此外，扩展表示亦可绕过参数更新：通过训练辅助目标动态检索当前上下文窗口外的“远古历史”片段并直接拼接，可在完全不更新核心语言模型参数的条件下显著降低困惑度[19]。

sections.title: 数据规模、配比与训练稳定性
sections.body:
语言模型规模规律的研究不仅局限于参数扩张，数据规模的有效性、混合配比的策略以及由此引发的训练稳定性问题同样构成了核心演进主线。随着预训练语料从单一来源向多源异构扩展，如何预测和优化数据组合成为重要议题。

在数据配比与泛化性能的机制方面，[28]通过最优实验设计理论推导出泛化误差的有理函数近似，将多数据源混合下的模型性能预测转化为学习问题，从而在大幅外推条件下也能有效预估性能。针对特定领域的配比，[36]基于法律判决数据集CaseHOLD的研究表明，当目标任务与预训练语料展现出充分的相似性与领域特异性时，投入大量资源进行特定领域预训练相比通用语料预训练（如基于谷歌图书和维基百科的通用BERT）能带来显著的性能增益。此外，为了让语言模型更好地捕获历史或地理分布的异质性，[48]并未采用直接切分数据集分别训练的传统方法，而是通过将元数据作为特殊Token直接注入掩码语言模型（MLM）的输入序列中。该机制表明，在特定比例（如25%）下对元数据进行掩码训练，不仅能引导模型学习文本内容与元数据的深层关联，还避免了为不同数据子集进行多次独立训练的成本。

数据重复度是影响大语言模型训练稳定性的另一个微观关键因素。[54]通过将宏观缩放规律与微观可解释性机制相结合指出，当预训练语料中存在少量被高频重复的数据时（例如0.1%的数据重复100次），会诱发强烈的基于轮次的“双重下降”（double descent）现象，导致训练中途测试损失异常上升。这种性能严重退化源于模型将大量表征容量耗费在记忆重复数据上，从而对负责泛化能力的内部机制（如归纳头）造成不成比例的破坏。

在数据组织结构的配比上，为了赋予自回归语言模型中间填充（FIM）能力，[40]通过文档级或上下文级的随机变换，将输入文本拆分为前缀、后缀和中间部分。实验证实，即使在预训练数据中混入高达50%的FIM变换格式数据，也完全不会对模型原有的从左到右自回归生成损失产生破坏。这证明了合理规划数据格式的混合比例，可以在不损失基础泛化性能的前提下，以零额外代价解锁模型的结构化生成新能力。

sections.title: 扩展规律和资源约束
sections.body:
语言模型规模规律的研究已从纯预训练阶段延伸至全生命周期及复杂资源约束下的机制演进。早期扩展规律曾假设自回归语言模型的性能主要依赖参数总规模而弱依赖网络形状。然而针对预训练-微调范式，实证表明下游微调任务的性能对模型形状高度敏感，且小模型的扩展经验无法直接迁移至大计算资源区间[30]。在给定计算预算下，将算力用于扩大模型尺寸的边际收益显著高于单纯延长训练步数，相较而言增加批次大小比增加步数更有益[12]。更进一步，针对特定架构的自回归Transformer，其解码器参数量与模型困惑度呈现出极高的秩相关性，这一规律直接促成了免训练的零成本架构搜索代理，大幅消减了模型结构搜索的算力消耗[46]。

随着模型向千亿参数演进，算力与显存瓶颈的物理表现发生转变。研究指出，在混合精度与检查点等机制支持下，限制大模型扩展的实质壁垒并非普遍假定的“内存墙”，而是极长的训练周期[25]。为突破时间与空间双重约束，分布式训练分化出多维并行与异构卸载两大优化分支。针对极大规模扩展，Megatron-Turing NLG 530B等模型采用深度融合数据、张量与流水线的3D并行架构跨节点扩展[58]；结合分层梯度累积与模块化流水线并行，可大幅降低分布式数据移动，使常规互联网络亦能承载原需高带宽通信的训练数据流[25]。针对单节点显存受限场景，ZeRO-Offload将优化器状态和参数更新计算卸载至CPU内存，并设计单步延迟参数更新机制（DPU）使得CPU与GPU计算重叠，从而在隐蔽通信开销的同时突破单卡显存极限[37]。

在面临极端序列长度或特殊分布式约束时，架构本身的运行机制需定向改造。处理超长上下文时，交错局部块与全局词元结合的稀疏注意力机制，配合先短序列后长序列的两阶段预训练适应，能在控制额外显存的同时有效提升长序列建模能力[45]。计算图动态性强的递归神经网络文法（RNNG）则通过跨句张量重组机制化解了传统批处理困难，实现了匹配计算硬件的张量并行扩展[15]。此外，在跨设备去中心化计算（如联邦学习）中，模型的拓扑压缩机制会直接影响扩展稳定性；例如采用知识蒸馏压缩的学生模型在多客户端联邦平均更新时，较其未蒸馏的庞大基础模型更容易出现收敛迟缓甚至性能崩溃[31]，凸显了分布式扩展下模型内部信息流转的脆弱性。

sections.title: 实验证据与方法比较
sections.body:
语言模型规模规律的评估标准在演进过程中，逐渐暴露出传统单一指标的局限性。早期的主流指标如困惑度（Perplexity）高度依赖于词频统计，容易受到自然语言中齐夫定律（Zipfian distribution）高频词的干扰，从而掩盖了模型在低频词或深层语义上的真实表现[7]。为了更细粒度地评估模型的生成质量，研究表明需要考察模型生成文本与真实自然语言在统计分布（如长度、停用词等）上的拟合度，并且这种拟合度受采样策略和架构的显著影响[22]。为此，评估基准逐渐从扁平化的数据集堆叠，演进为包含“语言能力-任务-数据集”层级架构[13]以及按难度分级的多任务生成评估体系[9]。

在不同对照条件下，模型规模扩展呈现出复杂的、甚至冲突的性能曲线。架构差异与下游任务适配方法是决定缩放规律形态的关键变量。在机器翻译等任务中，不同掩码机制的语言模型与编码器-解码器架构在小参数规模下表现出显著的性能鸿沟，但随着参数量级向大基数扩展，这种由架构引入的性能差距会逐渐缩小[43]。另一方面，针对分布外数据的组合泛化任务，模型扩展并非总是带来收益：全参数微调通常表现出平坦甚至负向的缩放曲线（大模型更易出现特定类型的过拟合），而提示微调（Prompt tuning）和上下文学习（In-context learning）则能维持正向的规模扩展收益[42]。

最为典型的冲突结果体现在“逆向缩放”（Inverse Scaling）现象及其机制中。部分基准测试曾指出某些任务性能随参数增加而下降。然而，当规模进一步扩大时，这种下降往往演变为“U型缩放”曲线[44]。该机制的本质在于任务包含了“真实任务”和“干扰任务”：中等规模模型具备了执行干扰任务的能力导致总体性能受损，只有大型模型才具备忽略干扰解决真实任务的涌现能力[44]。此外，这种曲线对评估对照条件极度敏感。在复杂推理任务中，若引入思维链（Chain-of-Thought）提示，原本在仅输出答案（Answer-only）条件下呈现平坦或逆向缩放的曲线会转为正向扩展，这证明了次优的提示对照会严重低估模型的真实能力[39][44]。

sections.title: 局限、效率与开放问题
sections.body:
规模规律的预测可靠性高度依赖拟合策略，相较于简单的插值，基于外推损失的方法能更准确地预测未见规模的性能[51]。尽管泛化误差随数据量呈现幂律递减，但模型最优参数量级与数据量之间实为亚线性扩展关系[3]。更为严峻的是数据供给极限，高质量文本数据可能在短期内耗尽，打破依赖海量数据扩展的现有范式[60]。此外，单纯的数据扩展会放大分布缺陷：当语料未经过滤时，规模扩大会导致生成更多攻击性文本[29]；在真实性问答中，由于模型过度拟合训练集中的“模仿性谬误”，更大规模的模型反而表现出更低的真实性[35]。同时，评估泄露问题也随着数据规模扩张而加剧，必须通过量化验证评估块与训练数据的重叠比例，以剥离纯记忆对规模收益的虚假贡献[20]。

在环境与算力成本日益高昂的压力下[21]，模型扩展暴露出诸多工程效率瓶颈。受限于硬件显存瓶颈与多维并行策略的节点跨越成本，参数规模在特定区间（如20B至70B）出现了由于成本效益骤降而导致的“参数真空”现象[47]。为在资源约束下突破基准缩放曲线，研究者在训练与部署端探索了多套机制：在训练阶段，利用混合降噪目标（Mixture-of-Denoisers）进行极少步数的持续训练，能够在不增加参数量的前提下显著提升下游性能曲线[57]；在推理阶段，动态条件计算架构允许模型根据不同计算预算实时切断或激活特定执行路径[8]，而针对混合专家（MoE）模型，将专家权重进行4位整数对称量化并结合推理时的融合反量化计算，有效化解了显存带宽限制并维持了计算精度[59]。然而，并非所有底层优化都能成功跨越规模鸿沟，旨在打破反向传播串行约束的直接反馈对齐（DFA）机制在因果解码器中始终无法获得超越反向传播的计算效率[53]，且常用于视觉的动态稀疏训练方法（如RigL）在大型语言模型中亦未能兑现降低浮点运算的理论预期[32]。

规模规律最深层的理论失效在于其无法解释预训练损失与下游特定任务间的“不可预测性”。尽管整体语言建模的交叉熵损失随计算规模平滑下降，但模型在复杂算术、多步推理等任务上的准确率却会在跨越某计算阈值时呈现不连续的突变式跃升[49]。这种宏观指标平滑与微观能力突变的并存机制[50]，部分源于精确匹配等离散指标未能反映出目标序列对数似然在小规模时的持续改善[41]。由于这种突发能力无法通过小规模模型的基准表现进行外推，其不仅为大模型的安全部署与风险审查带来了盲区[50]，也使得揭示模型如何将量变转化为涌现能力的微观机制，成为当前规律研究中最具挑战性的开放问题。
